questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The receptor used by HIV to enter CD4 lymphocytes, in addition to CD4 itself, is:
questions.concept: Gp120 binds CD4 and then a chemokine co-receptor - CCR5 for macrophage-tropic strains transmitted early, CXCR4 for T-tropic strains later. Homozygous CCR5-delta32 deletion confers near-complete resistance.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: As per current national guidelines, antiretroviral therapy in an HIV-positive adult is started:
options: At the time of diagnosis irrespective of CD4 count
questions.concept: Test-and-treat is now universal: ART begins at diagnosis regardless of CD4 count or clinical stage, which reduces morbidity, mortality and transmission. The preferred first-line regimen in India is tenofovir, lamivudine and dolutegravir.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis against Pneumocystis pneumonia is indicated when the CD4 count falls below:
questions.concept: Primary prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole starts at a CD4 count below 200 per microlitre, and also protects against toxoplasmosis and some bacterial infections. It may be stopped once CD4 is sustained above 200 on ART.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The commonest cause of a ring-enhancing space-occupying brain lesion in an AIDS patient is:
questions.concept: Toxoplasma encephalitis typically gives multiple ring-enhancing lesions with a predilection for the basal ganglia; empirical pyrimethamine with sulfadiazine and folinic acid is standard, with lymphoma considered if there is no response.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Cryptococcal meningitis in AIDS is best diagnosed by:
options: India ink preparation and cryptococcal antigen testing of cerebrospinal fluid
questions.concept: Cryptococcus neoformans is demonstrated by India ink showing capsulated budding yeast, with cryptococcal antigen being more sensitive; mucicarmine stains the capsule. Treatment is amphotericin B with flucytosine followed by fluconazole.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Oral hairy leukoplakia in an HIV-positive patient is caused by:
questions.concept: Oral hairy leukoplakia consists of corrugated white plaques on the lateral tongue that cannot be scraped off, caused by Epstein-Barr virus - unlike candidal thrush, which is removable.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Which malignancy is an AIDS-defining illness associated with human herpesvirus 8?
questions.concept: Kaposi sarcoma is driven by HHV-8 and appears as violaceous plaques or nodules on skin, palate and viscera. Cervical carcinoma and primary CNS lymphoma are the other AIDS-defining malignancies.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome typically occurs:
options: Within weeks to months of starting antiretroviral therapy as CD4 recovers
questions.concept: As immune function recovers, a paradoxical inflammatory worsening of a treated or subclinical infection - classically tuberculosis or cryptococcosis - occurs within weeks to months. ART is continued and steroids are given if severe.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Which antiretroviral drug is associated with proximal renal tubular dysfunction and reduced bone mineral density?
questions.concept: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate causes proximal tubulopathy including Fanconi syndrome and reduces bone density; zidovudine causes anaemia and myopathy, nevirapine hepatitis and rash, and dolutegravir weight gain.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The window period for HIV infection refers to the interval between:
options: Exposure and appearance of detectable antibody
questions.concept: The window period is the interval after infection when the person is infectious but antibody tests are still negative; fourth-generation p24 antigen-antibody assays and nucleic acid testing shorten it considerably.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: Septic shock is currently defined as sepsis with:
options: Persisting hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP 65 mmHg or more with lactate above 2 mmol/L
questions.concept: Sepsis-3 defines sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction (SOFA rise of 2 or more) from a dysregulated host response, and septic shock as vasopressor-dependent hypotension with hyperlactataemia despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: The single most important intervention that improves survival in septic shock is:
options: Early appropriate antibiotics with source control and fluid resuscitation
questions.concept: Each hour of delay in effective antibiotics increases mortality, so cultures are taken and broad-spectrum antibiotics given within the first hour together with 30 mL/kg of crystalloid and source control.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: The vasopressor of first choice in septic shock is:
questions.concept: Noradrenaline is first line because it raises mean arterial pressure through alpha-1 vasoconstriction with less tachyarrhythmia than dopamine; vasopressin is added as a second agent to spare the noradrenaline dose.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: Fever of unknown origin is classically defined as fever above 38.3 degrees Celsius for at least:
options: Three weeks with no diagnosis after appropriate investigation
questions.concept: The classical Petersdorf definition requires temperature above 38.3 degrees on several occasions for more than three weeks with no diagnosis after appropriate inpatient or outpatient investigation. Infection, malignancy and connective tissue disease are the three broad groups.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: The commonest infective cause of fever of unknown origin in India is:
questions.concept: Extrapulmonary and disseminated tuberculosis is the leading infective cause of prolonged fever in India, often with normal chest radiography, so tissue diagnosis and imaging of the abdomen are important.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: Raised serum procalcitonin is most useful in:
options: Distinguishing bacterial from viral infection and guiding antibiotic de-escalation
questions.concept: Procalcitonin rises in bacterial sepsis and falls with resolution, so serial values help decide when antibiotics can safely be stopped - a key stewardship tool. It is not specific enough to start or withhold antibiotics alone.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: The core principle of antimicrobial stewardship on receiving culture sensitivity results is:
options: De-escalation to the narrowest effective agent
questions.concept: Stewardship means starting broad when the patient is septic and then de-escalating to the narrowest effective agent for the shortest adequate duration, which limits resistance, cost and Clostridioides difficile infection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: Which is a component of the quick SOFA (qSOFA) score?
options: Respiratory rate 22 or more per minute
questions.concept: qSOFA uses three bedside items: respiratory rate 22 or more, altered mentation (GCS below 15) and systolic blood pressure 100 mmHg or less. Two or more identifies patients at risk of poor outcome without needing laboratory tests.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: Empirical antibiotic cover for febrile neutropenia should include activity against:
questions.concept: Antipseudomonal cover, for example piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime, is mandatory within an hour of presentation because Pseudomonas bacteraemia in neutropenia is rapidly fatal. Antifungals are added for persistent fever after 4 to 7 days.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Sepsis, fever of unknown origin & antimicrobial stewardship
questions.stem: A patient develops profuse diarrhoea after prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics. The likely organism and treatment are:
options: Clostridioides difficile treated with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin
questions.concept: Antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis is caused by toxigenic Clostridioides difficile; the offending antibiotic is stopped and oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin given. Metronidazole is now second line.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Leptospirosis is most commonly transmitted to humans through:
options: Contact of abraded skin or mucosa with water contaminated by rodent urine
questions.concept: Leptospira interrogans is shed in rodent urine and penetrates abraded skin or mucous membranes during contact with contaminated flood water, making it an occupational and monsoon-related disease of farmers and sewage workers.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Weil's disease refers to severe leptospirosis with:
options: Jaundice, acute kidney injury and haemorrhage
questions.concept: Weil's disease is the icteric form with conjunctival suffusion, jaundice, acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia and pulmonary haemorrhage; treatment is intravenous penicillin or ceftriaxone, with doxycycline for mild disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: An eschar at the site of a mite bite with fever, lymphadenopathy and raised transaminases suggests:
questions.concept: Orientia tsutsugamushi is transmitted by the chigger of the Leptotrombidium mite and produces a painless eschar with regional lymphadenopathy; doxycycline or azithromycin gives a dramatic response within 48 hours.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The Weil-Felix test is used in the diagnosis of:
questions.concept: The Weil-Felix test detects antibodies cross-reacting with Proteus OX-19, OX-2 and OX-K antigens in rickettsial disease. It is cheap but insensitive and non-specific; immunofluorescence assay is the reference standard.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The drug of choice for scrub typhus in a non-pregnant adult is:
questions.concept: Doxycycline is the drug of choice for all rickettsial infections, with azithromycin preferred in pregnancy and children. Beta-lactams are ineffective as these are obligate intracellular organisms.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Brucellosis is characteristically associated with:
options: Undulant fever with sacroiliitis and hepatosplenomegaly
questions.concept: Brucellosis, acquired from unpasteurised milk or animal contact, causes undulant fever, drenching sweats, sacroiliitis and hepatosplenomegaly with a normal or low white cell count; treatment is doxycycline with rifampicin or streptomycin for six weeks.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The most important reservoir for rabies in India is:
questions.concept: The dog accounts for the overwhelming majority of human rabies in India. Rabies is virtually 100% fatal once symptomatic, so category III bites need wound washing, rabies immunoglobulin and a full vaccine course.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Negri bodies in rabies are found in the:
options: Cytoplasm of neurons, especially hippocampal pyramidal and cerebellar Purkinje cells
questions.concept: Negri bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions of viral nucleocapsid, most abundant in hippocampal pyramidal cells and cerebellar Purkinje cells, and are pathognomonic though present in only about 70% of cases.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The vector of plague is:
questions.concept: Yersinia pestis is transmitted by the rat flea Xenopsylla cheopis, causing bubonic plague with a tender matted bubo; pneumonic plague spreads person to person by droplets and is the most lethal form.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Which zoonosis is classically transmitted by contact with infected animal products and forms a painless black necrotic eschar?
questions.concept: Cutaneous anthrax from Bacillus anthracis produces a painless malignant pustule with a black eschar and marked oedema, typically in handlers of hides, wool or carcasses; treatment is ciprofloxacin or doxycycline.
